keyPoints: Natural vegetative propagation: happens on its own, from the parent's own structures (roots, stems, leaves, runners, bulbs); no human input.
Artificial vegetative propagation: human-directed, using a removed 'vegetative propagule' (e.g. stem cuttings, grafting, tissue culture/micropropagation).
Both give genetically identical offspring to the parent.
Artificial methods (especially tissue culture) are generally better/faster for large-scale rapid propagation than relying on natural methods alone.
modelAnswer: Vegetative propagation (natural vegetative propagation) is the process by which plants reproduce asexually on their own, using their own natural mechanisms without human intervention; new plants develop directly from vegetative structures of the parent plant such as roots, stems, leaves, runners, or bulbs, and because they come from the same parent, they carry identical genetic characteristics. Artificial vegetative propagation, by contrast, is used when people purposely propagate plants to meet specific needs (such as preserving good qualities like taste, colour, or disease resistance); it relies on a deliberately removed part of the plant, called a vegetative propagule, using methods such as stem cuttings and grafting that humans carry out rather than the plant achieving on its own. Which is better for rapid propagation: artificial vegetative propagation is generally better for rapid, large-scale propagation, because methods such as stem cuttings, grafting, and especially tissue culture (micropropagation) let growers deliberately and quickly produce large numbers of genetically identical plants under controlled conditions, whereas natural vegetative propagation depends on the plant's own slower, structure-by-structure growth (such as suckers or bulbs forming over time).

modelAnswer: Cloning is a method of producing genetically identical individuals from a single parental cell. In plants, cloning refers to tissue culturing (also called micropropagation): a single plant cell or piece of tissue (the explant) is grown on an artificial nutrient medium under aseptic conditions to develop a genetically identical copy of the parent plant. Tissue culturing (plant cloning) is the process of a plant that is considered a form of cloning.

modelAnswer: Apomixis: asexual formation of a seed from the ovule's own tissues, without meiosis or fertilization; also called parthenogenesis. Pollination: transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. Male gametophyte: the germinated pollen grain, with its tube nucleus and two sperm nuclei. Epigeal germination: the hypocotyl elongates, pulling the cotyledons above ground (e.g. beans). Fertilization: fusion of a sperm nucleus with the egg to form a zygote. Binary fission: a cell splits into two identical daughter cells (e.g. bacteria). Budding: a small outgrowth on the parent grows and may detach as a new individual (e.g. yeast). Sporangiophores: stalks bearing spore-producing sacs (sporangia), as in Rhizopus. Rootstock: the lower part of a graft, giving roots and stem support. Bulb: a thickened underground stem wrapped in fleshy storage leaves (e.g. onion). Rhizome: a horizontal underground stem with nodes bearing shoots and roots (e.g. ginger).

modelAnswer: (a) Asexual: single parent, clones, no gametes/meiosis. Sexual: fusion of gametes from two parents, varied offspring. (b) Natural vegetative propagation: no human role (runners, bulbs, rhizomes, suckers). Artificial: human-driven (cuttings, grafting). (c) Scion: upper graft part with desired traits. Rootstock: lower part, gives roots and support. (d) Grafting: joins a scion to a separate rootstock. Stem cutting: one piece of stem grows its own roots. (e) Bulb: thickened underground stem wrapped in fleshy leaves (onion). Rhizome: horizontal underground stem with nodes (ginger). (f) Binary fission: one cell splits into two (bacteria). Budding: an outgrowth enlarges and may detach (yeast). (g) Hypogeal: epicotyl elongates, cotyledons stay underground (peas). Epigeal: hypocotyl elongates, cotyledons rise above ground (beans). (h) Self pollination: within the same flower or plant. Cross pollination: between two separate plants, more genetic variability.

modelAnswer: Plant tissue culture (cloning/micropropagation) procedure: (1) A single cell or small piece of tissue is taken from the parent plant; this starting piece is called the explant. (2) The explant is placed on an artificial nutrient medium under aseptic (microbe-free) conditions. (3) The explant's cells divide repeatedly to form an undifferentiated mass of cells called a callus. (4) The callus is treated with plant growth substances to make it first produce shoots, then roots, giving a young plantlet. (5) The plantlets are carefully transferred into soil in natural conditions to continue growing into full plants, each genetically identical to the parent.

modelAnswer: Binary fission (bacteria): a copy of the bacterium's DNA is made so there are two identical sets, which move to opposite ends of the cell. The middle of the cell folds inward, dividing the contents into two, and a new cell wall forms between them, producing two identical daughter bacteria. Budding (yeast): a small outgrowth (bud) forms on one side of the parent yeast cell. The nucleus divides by mitosis into two, and one nucleus moves into the bud. The bud enlarges and comes to resemble the parent; it may then detach as a separate individual, or in some cases stay attached, forming a small connected group of cells.

modelAnswer: Two methods of artificial vegetative propagation: (1) Stem cuttings: a small segment of stem with at least one node is placed in water or damp soil; roots grow from the buried end while the top continues growing leaves. If growth does not start, the cut end is treated with the plant hormone auxin to stimulate rooting; this method is used for roses, ivy, grapevines and chrysanthemums. (2) Grafting: two plant parts are joined to make one new plant. The scion (upper part, carrying the desired fruit/flower traits) is cut and attached to the rootstock (lower part, providing roots and stem support), usually at matching angled cuts, and bound (e.g. with grafting tape) until the graft heals; used for fruit trees and ornamental plants.
stem: Describe any two methods of artificial vegetative propagation in plants.

modelAnswer: Natural vegetative propagation happens without human help, using the plant's own structures: (1) Bulbs: thickened underground stems wrapped in fleshy leaves; shoots from the top and roots from the base grow into new plants (onion, tulip). (2) Corms: thickened underground stems without fleshy leaves; buds at the top give rise to shoots (garlic, dasheen). (3) Rhizomes: horizontal underground stems with nodes; buds on top grow shoots, the underside grows roots (ginger). (4) Stem tubers: swollen underground stem tips with bud 'eyes' that sprout new shoots (potato). (5) Stolons/runners: horizontal stems that grow along the ground from the parent; each node can root and shoot into a new plant (strawberry). (6) Suckers: shoots arising from underground roots or the stem base that become independent plants (lawn grass). (7) Leaves: in Bryophyllum, plantlets form along leaf edges and grow into new plants after falling to the soil.

keyPoints: One sperm nucleus + egg cell -> diploid zygote.
Other sperm nucleus + polar nuclei/secondary nucleus -> triploid endosperm nucleus.
Called 'double' because one male gametophyte's two sperm nuclei each carry out a separate fusion; unique to angiosperms.
modelAnswer: When the pollen tube penetrates the ovule, the male gametophyte releases two sperm nuclei. One sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, while the other sperm nucleus fuses with the polar nuclei (or secondary nucleus) to form a triploid endosperm nucleus, which develops into the nutritive endosperm tissue. Because one male gametophyte contributes two sperm nuclei that each carry out a separate fusion in this way, the event is called double fertilization, a feature unique to flowering plants (angiosperms).

keyPoints: Pollen grain (microspore) germinates on the stigma after pollination.
Microspore nucleus divides by mitosis into a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus.
Generative nucleus divides again into two sperm nuclei.
Tube nucleus directs pollen-tube growth through the style into the ovule.
Male gametophyte = microspore body + pollen tube + tube nucleus + two sperm nuclei.
modelAnswer: A flowering plant's life cycle alternates between a diploid sporophyte generation and a haploid gametophyte generation. On the sporophyte, pollen grains (microspores) form in the anther; after pollination, a microspore germinates on the stigma surface to begin forming the male gametophyte. The microspore nucleus first divides by mitosis to form two nuclei: a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus. The generative nucleus divides again to produce two sperm nuclei. The tube nucleus controls the growth of the pollen tube, which the microspore forms as it grows down through the style and eventually penetrates the ovule. The complete structure made up of the microspore body, the pollen tube, the tube nucleus, and the two sperm nuclei together is called the male gametophyte. (Sketch: draw the flower life cycle with the sporophyte (mature flowering plant) producing pollen grains in the anther, a germinating pollen grain forming a pollen tube growing down the style toward the ovule, with the tube nucleus and two sperm nuclei labelled inside it.)

keyPoints: Functional megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis 3 times -> 8 nuclei.
3 nuclei at one end: egg cell (centre) + 2 synergids.
3 nuclei at the other end: antipodals.
2 remaining nuclei in the centre: polar nuclei (may fuse into a secondary nucleus).
Female gametophyte (embryo sac) = megaspore body + 3 antipodals + 2 synergids + polar nuclei + egg.
modelAnswer: In the flowering-plant life cycle, the female gametophyte develops inside the ovule. The nucleus of the functional megaspore, located in the centre of the ovule, divides three times by mitosis to produce 8 nuclei. Of these, three nuclei migrate to one end of the ovule: the central one becomes the egg cell, and the two beside it become the synergids. Three other nuclei migrate to the opposite end and become the antipodals. The two remaining nuclei stay in the centre of the ovule and are called the polar nuclei; in some cases these two fuse together into a single diploid secondary nucleus before the sperm arrives. The complete structure, made up of the megaspore body, the three antipodals, the two synergids, the polar nuclei (or fused secondary nucleus), and the egg cell, together is called the female gametophyte, or embryo sac. (Sketch: draw the ovule containing the embryo sac with the egg cell and two synergids at the micropylar end, the two polar nuclei in the centre, and the three antipodal cells at the opposite (chalazal) end.)

modelAnswer: Two suitable conditions required for seed germination are: (1) Water (moisture): the seed must absorb water from its surroundings, which is used to break down stored food and activate growth of the embryo's parts. (2) Temperature: seeds need a suitable temperature range to germinate; for most plants this is between 25-30°C. (Oxygen is a third valid condition: the embryo's cells need it to respire.)

modelAnswer: The embryonic stem is part of the embryo inside a seed, running above and below the point where the cotyledon(s) attach. The portion above the cotyledon attachment point is called the epicotyl, and it grows into the plant's shoot. The portion below the cotyledon attachment point is called the hypocotyl. Together with the radicle (embryonic root, which grows into the new root) and plumule (embryonic shoot tip), the embryonic stem forms the axis of the seed embryo that develops into the young plant during germination.

modelAnswer: When the pollen tube penetrates the ovule, one of its two sperm nuclei fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, and the other sperm nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei (or the fused secondary nucleus) to form a triploid endosperm nucleus. Because a single male gametophyte contributes two sperm nuclei that each fuse with a different nucleus in the embryo sac, this event is called double fertilization. It is unique to flowering plants (angiosperms) and produces both the zygote (which becomes the embryo) and the endosperm nucleus (which becomes the nutritive endosperm tissue of the seed).

modelAnswer: The embryo sac is the female gametophyte of a flowering plant, formed inside the ovule. The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides three times by mitosis to produce 8 nuclei. Three of these migrate to one end of the ovule: the central one becomes the egg cell, flanked by two synergids. Three other nuclei migrate to the opposite end and become the antipodals. The remaining two nuclei move to the centre of the ovule as polar nuclei, which may fuse into a single diploid secondary nucleus before fertilization. So the embryo sac consists of 1 egg cell, 2 synergids, 3 antipodals, and 2 polar nuclei (or 1 secondary nucleus), 8 nuclei in total.

modelAnswer: Sexual reproduction is more beneficial than asexual reproduction because it involves the fusion of gametes from two different parents, which mixes and shuffles genetic material through meiosis. This produces offspring that are genetically varied rather than exact clones. Cross pollination, in particular, ensures more genetic variability in successive generations. This variability gives a population a greater range of traits to draw on, improving its ability to adapt and survive changing conditions, which asexual reproduction (offspring genetically identical to a single parent) cannot provide.

modelAnswer: Male gametophyte: after pollination, a pollen grain (microspore) germinates on the stigma. Its nucleus divides by mitosis into a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus; the generative nucleus divides again to form two sperm nuclei. The tube nucleus directs growth of the pollen tube down through the style into the ovule. The whole structure (microspore body, pollen tube, tube nucleus, and two sperm nuclei) is the male gametophyte. Female gametophyte (embryo sac): the functional megaspore's nucleus inside the ovule divides three times by mitosis to give 8 nuclei. Three migrate to one end (the central one becomes the egg, flanked by two synergids); three migrate to the other end (the antipodals); the remaining two become polar nuclei at the centre, which may fuse into a diploid secondary nucleus. This whole structure (egg, 2 synergids, 3 antipodals, 2 polar nuclei/secondary nucleus) is the female gametophyte, or embryo sac.

modelAnswer: Seed germination is the process by which a seed absorbs water, swells, breaks its seed coat, and grows into a seedling, marking the start of a new plant's life. There are two types: (1) Epigeal germination, where the hypocotyl elongates and forms a hook that pulls the cotyledons above the ground (e.g. beans, cotton, papaya). (2) Hypogeal germination, where the epicotyl elongates and forms the hook while the cotyledons stay underground (e.g. peas, maize, coconut). Conditions needed for germination: internally, the seed must contain a living embryo and enough stored food; externally, it needs water (moisture, to soak the seed and mobilize stored food), oxygen (for the embryo's cells to respire), and a suitable temperature (about 25-30°C for most plants).

modelAnswer: A typical flower consists of a stalk (pedicel) that holds it up, topped by a swollen platform called the thalamus. The thalamus bears four whorls of floral leaves. The outermost whorl is the calyx, made of green sepals that protect the inner parts. Just inside is the corolla, made of coloured petals. The calyx and corolla take no direct part in reproduction, so together they are called the accessory whorls. Inside the corolla is the androecium (the male whorl), made of stamens that produce pollen; each stamen has a filament and an anther containing pollen sacs. At the centre is the gynoecium (the female whorl), made of one or more carpels/pistils, each with an ovary (containing ovules), a style, and a stigma. The androecium and gynoecium actually carry out reproduction, so they are called the necessary whorls.
